# Draft:Maurice Ward (radio personality)

Maurice Ward (born January 1, 1942), also known on air as “The Magnificent Maurice,” “Mr. Rhythm,” and “Beast from the East,” is an American radio and television personality., political consultant, and music producer from Huntersville, Virginia. He worked in broadcasting for more than six decades and is known for his role in historically Black radio, particularly Norfolk Virginia’s historic black-oriented radio station WRAP.
Ward broadcasted live programming both nationally and internationally,  including hosting programs at WRAP, as well as WKQA/WYRM and WLPM  in Virginia, KAPE in San Antonio, Texas, and ZFB Radio in Bermuda.
As a music producer and label operator, Ward worked with soul, rhythm-and-blues and gospel artists during the 1970s through his Norfolk Sound, LaShawn Records , Jerusalem Records and Rose Ward Music   , including being credited as producer on Lee Field's popular hit “[https://genius.com/Lee-fields-lets-talk-it-over-lyrics Let’s Talk it Over]” He was also credited as a co-writer on the 1972 song “Everybody Gonna Give Their Thing Away to Somebody (Sometime)”  by both Lee Fields and Jerry Williams, as well as a producer on Fields’s recording “She’s a Love Maker.”
As a musician, Ward released two songs “Then You can Tell me Goodbye”  and  “The Sexy Groove” on his label LaShawn records
Ward has also been active in Virginia politics, worked as a campaign manager and consultant on local, state, and national political campaigns, including the successful mayoral campaign of William E. “Bill” Ward,  Chesapeake’s first African American and longest-serving mayor. Ward wrote a weekly column for the “Clipper,” an insert of the Virginian-Pilot, where he often endorsed candidates for office. His politically centered radio talk show “The Hampton Roads Crier” was frequented by elected officials Virginia candidates on the campaign trail for local, state and U.S. offices for over a decade.
Early Life
Early life
On January 1, 1942, Maurice Ward was born to Olendus Ward Sr. and his wife Thelma Elizabeth Ward (Freeman) in Huntersville, Virginia. He grew up in a small, predominantly black community in Nansemond County, Virginia surrounded by local farms that provided income and food for the local residents.
After attending East Suffolk high school, Ward transferred to Crestwood High School  which was at the time a newly designated high school for black children in Norfolk County prior to integration. Ward graduated from Crestwood High School in 1960.
He later enrolled at Norfolk division of Virginia State College of Petersburg, Virginia, now Norfolk State University and attended the Radio Engineering Institute of Electronics in Sarasota, Florida, before earning an associate degree in management from Tidewater Community College in 1976.
Broadcasting Career
Early Years
Ward began his broadcasting career in 1961 as a teenage announcer at WRAP Radio in Norfolk. At the time, WRAP was among a limited number of American radio stations broadcasting full-time programming primarily for African American audiences. Immediately after graduating from high school, he began on-air training under John “Daddy Jack” Albert Holmes Jr., Virginia’s first Black disc jockey, and among the original thirteen in the country.
During his early training period, Ward read weather reports and assisted with programming. While appearing on a teen-oriented program at WRAP, he co-hosted segments with DJ Bobby J and Beverly Sykes that included reading letters submitted by students from surrounding communities.
Ward’s service in the United States Air Force as a sales specialist led to broadcasting roles in other parts of the United States and abroad, including in San Antonio, Texas, and in Bermuda.
During his early broadcasting years, he used the on-air name “Mr. Rhythm” before adopting the names “The Magnificent Maurice” and “Beast from the East” after returning to WRAP in the late 1960s.
Radio Career and Influence
Ward worked at several radio stations in Virginia and beyond over the course of his career.
From 1964 to 1965, Ward worked at KAPE (1480 AM) in San Antonio, Texas. He then served as an announcer at ZFB Radio in Bermuda from 1965 to 1966.
He was associated primarily with WRAP in Norfolk, where he hosted programs under on-air names including “Magnificent Maurice” and “Beast from the East.” His programming followed the tenure of Jack Holmes and aired primarily during weekday and weeknight time slots.
During the 1970s and 1980s, Ward hosted a weeknight radio program on WRAP that featured rhythm-and-blues, soul music, and community-oriented programming. At WRAP, he worked alongside other notable announcers, including Jack Holmes and Leola Dyson. He also hosted record hops and gospel programs at local high schools and churches in the Tidewater area.
Ward served as the station’s program director and music director in the mid-1970s.
In 1990, Ward worked as a gospel announcer at WLPM (1450 AM) in Suffolk, Virginia.
Ward is credited with providing training to other radio announcers and future journalists, including Chuck King, David Frank, Columbus Kellam, Darryl Cox, and Brandi Kellam, among others.
Ward also co-sponsored and helped lead a broadcast club at Western Branch Middle School and High School, which awarded scholarships to student participants.
In 2023, Ward helped establish the WRAP Historic Society and has served as its president. The organization focuses on preserving and documenting the history of Black radio and broadcasters in the Hampton Roads region.
The Hampton Roads Crier
In 2007, Ward launched The Hampton Roads Crier, a call-in public affairs radio program airing on WYRM and WKQA AM 1110 in Norfolk, Virgina. The show was sponsored by Little Joe's Autos, an automobile dealership in the Virginia Tidewater region owned by Joseph A. Falk, and focused on political and civic issues.
From 2009 to 2011, Ward co-hosted the program with journalist Brandi Kellam, who later became an Emmy Award–winning investigative journalist and filmmaker.
The program regularly featured elected officials, candidates for public office, and community leaders, including former U.S. Representative J. Randy Forbes, Virginia State Senator L. Louise Lucas, former State Senator Harry B. Blevins, Chesapeake’s first Black and longest-serving mayor William E. “Bill” Ward , and Terry McAuliffe, who later served as governor of Virginia.
The show used a call-in format that allowed listeners to participate in discussions.
Ward retired from The Hampton Roads Crier and concluded his radio career in 2022 after fifteen years.
He was inducted as a 2024 honoree into the Hampton Roads Black Radio Announcers Association Wall of Fame, an honor celebrating local Black radio legends in the Hampton Roads area.
Political Career and Consulting
Political Career
Ward became involved in Virginia political consulting and campaign work in the 1970s. He chaired the election committee that helped elect Dr. Hugo A. Owens  as one of Chesapeake’s first Black members of the City Council in 1970.
In 1978, Ward ran for a seat on the Chesapeake City Council and lost by approximately 900 votes.
From 1978 through 1992, Ward managed and coordinated political campaigns at the local level, including serving as campaign manager and advisor for William E. “Bill” Ward during his long-serving mayoral tenure.
In the late 1980s, Ward formed a political consulting company  and worked as a media and campaign consultant for candidates at both the local and state levels. His political work included advising and supporting elected officials and candidates from both major parties, including serving as legislative assistant to former Virginia State Delegate V. Thomas Forehand Jr. from 1988 to 1990, helping coordinate former State Senator Dick Saslaw’s 1989 lieutenant governor campaign as a liaison in Virginia’s 4th Congressional District
, and serving as a volunteer coordinator for former U.S. Representative J. Randy Forbes’s 2001 special election campaign for Congress.
Between 1988 and 1990, Ward wrote a weekly newspaper column for The Chesapeake Clipper, a community publication, titled Through My Eyes. His columns addressed local politics, civic issues, Black History Month, and community affairs.
Work with William E. “Bill” Ward
Maurice Ward and Chesapeake Mayor William E. “Bill” Ward developed a long-standing professional relationship beginning in the late 1970s, when Maurice Ward became involved in Bill Ward’s political campaigns and later served as a senior campaign advisor. Ward worked closely with Bill Ward during his successful campaign to become Chesapeake’s first Black mayor.
During this period, Maurice Ward coordinated and managed multiple local campaigns and remained involved in campaign strategy throughout Bill Ward’s elected career.
While Bill Ward served on city council, Maurice Ward received several appointments from the Chesapeake City Council, including service on the Industrial Development Authority, the Planning Commission, where he held roles as secretary and vice chairman, the Juvenile Advisory Board, and the Economic Development Authority, where he served as secretary.
Bill Ward also appeared as a guest on The Hampton Roads Crier. Following Bill Ward’s death in 2018, Maurice Ward dedicated an episode of the program to his public service and political career.
Maurice Ward is not related to William E. “Bill” Ward.
Music and Recording Work
Ward was involved in music production and songwriting in addition to his broadcasting career. During the 1970s, he worked on recordings by soul, funk, and gospel artists released through the Norfolk Sound, LaShawn Records, and Jerusalem Record Co. labels.
He collaborated with American soul singer Lee Fields on several recordings during this period, including “She’s a Love Maker” and “Let’s Talk It Over,” and was a co-writer on the 1972 song “Everybody Gonna Give Their Thing Away to Somebody (Sometime)” by Fields and Jerry Williams.
Through LaShawn Records, Ward released recordings by artists including Shirley Johnson and Reginald Milton and the Soul Jets. He also released recordings on the Norfolk Sound label, including work by Van Jones and the Jays in 1978.
He also produced gospel recordings through Jerusalem Record Co., including releases by The Gospel Gents in 1973. Ward later established the music publishing company Rose Ward Music, which published songs recorded by artists associated with his labels.
As a performer, he released the single “Then You Can Tell Me Goodbye” backed with “The Sexy Groove,” credited to The Magnificent Maurice Ward.
Personal Life
Personal Life
Ward married Rose Marie Ward  on June 30 1967 and they have five children including Rosnell, Eulene, Shannon, Teresa, and Maurice Lashawn Ward.
